title: Ultra-Peripheral Collisions as a Nuclear-Structure Interferometer with Interpretable Multitask Deep Learning
authors: Jing-Zong Zhang, Wang-Mei Zha, Lingxiao Wang, Guo-Liang Ma
abstract: Precise knowledge of nuclear structure is essential across fundamental physics, yet probing these structures is notoriously difficult. To address this challenge, ultra-peripheral collisions (UPCs) provide a femtoscopic tomography for imaging the atomic nucleus. UPCs offer a pristine electromagnetic pathway: coherent vector-meson photoproduction generates patterns of diffraction and two-source interference that directly encode the nuclear spatial density. Turning these patterns into quantitative constraints is, however, a challenging inverse problem, complicated by correlated sensitivities to deformation and neutron skin, phase smearing, and experimental backgrounds. Here we introduce an interpretable Multitask deep-learning framework that maps transverse momentum distributions to multiple nuclear-structure indicators simultaneously and identifies the kinematic regions driving each inference. We demonstrate the approach with coherent $J/ψ$ photoproduction in $^{96}_{40}\text{Zr} + ^{96}_{40}\text{Zr}$ collisions, showing that the learned features separate diffraction-dominated and interference-dominated information and provide analysis-ready observables for future high-luminosity data.
summary: This work treats ultra-peripheral collisions as a quantum interferometer to probe subtle details of nuclear structure. It introduces an interpretable multitask deep learning model that analyzes the resulting transverse momentum distributions. This framework successfully disentangles overlapping signatures, allowing researchers to simultaneously constrain both nuclear shape deformation and neutron skin thickness.
main_problem: Precisely determining nuclear structure parameters like shape deformation ($ eta_2$) and neutron skin thickness is difficult because these signatures are entangled in classical scattering observables.
main_result: The proposed interpretable Multitask deep-learning framework successfully disentangles the signals, allowing for simultaneous extraction of both quadrupole deformation and neutron-skin thickness from transverse momentum distributions.
method: A multitask deep learning model is trained on simulated 2D transverse momentum spectra to map complex interference patterns directly to multiple physical structure indicators.
model_or_system: The system uses Ultra-Peripheral Collisions (UPCs) as a femtoscopic interferometer, analyzing coherent vector-meson photoproduction ($J/\psi$) in heavy nuclei like $^{96}	ext{Zr}$. The physics is modeled using deformed Woods–Saxon profiles for the nuclear density.
key_observables: Transverse momentum distributions ($ rac{d^2P}{dp_x dp_y}$), which are analyzed to separate interference-dominated (deformation) and diffraction-dominated (neutron skin) information.
important_parameters: Quadrupole deformation ($ eta_2$), Octupole deformation ($ eta_3$), Neutron Skin Type, Transverse Momentum ($p_\perp$).
main_assumptions: The method assumes that the deep learning framework can learn a nonlinear inverse mapping robust enough to overcome holographic degeneracy and detector smearing.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the process from nuclear structure input to UPC interference patterns in $p_\perp$ space, showing how dark fringes relate to deformation ($ eta$) and bright spots relate to neutron skin. The model's attention maps (PDA) are used to localize these distinct physical signals.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical problem using UPCs as interferometers; it details the theoretical framework linking nuclear structure to $p_\perp$ spectra; it introduces the multitask deep learning architecture; and finally, it demonstrates parameter extraction robustness against background noise by mapping results back to measurable flow coefficients ($v_n$) and yield ratios.
why_interesting: The application of advanced ML techniques (multitask learning) to interpret complex quantum interference patterns in high-energy nuclear physics is a novel intersection between AI and fundamental structure determination, providing new tools for analyzing data from facilities like the LHC or EIC.

Figure 2 displays the simulated J/ψ photoproduction probability in the transverse momentum plane at mid-rapidity (y = 0) with b = 12 fm. Focusing on the coherent process in Fig. 2(a), within the transverse momentum range px, py ∈[−0.17, 0.17] GeV/c, the distribution exhibits a clear interference pattern characterized by a central dark fringe situated between a pair of bright spots. Experimental measurements are inherently contaminated by incoherent photoproduction, in which the photon inter- acts with an individual nucleon and breaks the coherence of the nucleus, often leading to nuclear dissociation.
